title: Data Synthesis for Alfalfa Biomass Yield Estimation
summary: Addresses the problem that a farm has too few local observations to train a yield model, and that training on non-local data from other states works no better than the scarce local data. The proposed pipeline, synthesized non-local training, fits a generator to abundant non-local records, samples a large synthetic training set from it, and classifies local yields with the result, gaining 42.9 percent accuracy over the best local or non-local baseline and topping out at 85.7 percent with a decision tree. The generators are CTGAN and TVAE taken from Xu et al., described in the paper by their mode-specific normalization and their conditional generator with training-by-sampling, and the two are compared throughout: CTGAN wins the headline result while TVAE is stronger when paired with gradient boosting. SDV's synthesizers are therefore the engine of the contribution rather than a comparison point.
evidence: the abstract states that the authors build on Xu et al. reference [5] by using their conditional tabular GAN (CTGAN) and tabular variational autoencoder (TVAE) synthesizers in the pipeline, and that the highest accuracy obtained from SNLT was 85.7 percent using a decision tree with CTGAN; the background states that CTGAN is called a conditional GAN because it uses a conditional generator and training-by-sampling to address class imbalance in discrete columns and introduces mode-specific normalization to normalize columns individually; tables 4 through 8 report local, non-local, SNLT (TVAE) and SNLT (CTGAN) accuracies side by side for seven classifiers; the discussion notes that although CTGAN consistently outperforms TVAE in reference [5], TVAE was competitive here, beating CTGAN in the SD and OH experiments

title: LFTD: Transformer-Enhanced Diffusion Model for Realistic Financial Time-Series Data Generation
summary: Targets financial statement data, where a static tabular block and a multi-year time series are entangled in one record and neither pure tabular nor pure sequence generators fit, and proposes LFTD, a diffusion model with a transformer refinement stage, evaluated on static and dynamic prediction of two market ratios. CTGAN is one of the generative augmentation baselines actually trained and sampled, alongside DDPM and a VAE, and the paper reports it performing poorly on this data, with low explained variance in the static setting and collapsing to zero or negative in the dynamic setting, which it reads as an inability to learn the structural properties of financial records. The related-work section credits CTGAN to Xu et al. for more stable distributional fidelity than conventional GANs on census income data. CTGAN is thus run only as the comparison the proposed model is measured against.
evidence: the related-work section lists SMOTE, CTGAN (reference 20), TableGAN and VAE-based models as the widely used tabular methods and states that CTGAN, proposed by Xu et al. (2019), demonstrated more stable distributional fidelity than conventional GANs on the UCI Adult Income dataset; the experimental design states that after selecting the best-performing variant the authors conduct additional comparisons against widely used data augmentation baselines including CTGAN, DDPM and VAE-based models; the results state that CTGAN performs poorly even in the static setting with low R2 values and that both DDPM and CTGAN drop to zero or negative R2 in the dynamic setting; tables 4 and 5 report CTGAN's RMSE, MAE, R2 and MAPE against the original data and the other generators

title: A Differential Approach to the Generation and Quality Assessment of Synthetic Data for Environmental Monitoring
summary: Asks which generator to choose when an environmental dataset is small, using a 297-sample geochemical table of 25 log-transformed elements, and compares a parametric Gaussian copula against TVAE on marginal fidelity, correlation preservation, privacy and a composite quality score, with a rare-earth subgroup analysis. GAN-based alternatives including CTGAN and CopulaGAN were deliberately excluded on the grounds that they need far more training data than field monitoring provides. The copula wins on global correlation preservation while TVAE better replicates marginals, holds local correlations and is harder to distinguish from real data. Both generators are SDV's, the paper naming the Synthetic Data Vault as the package through which the Gaussian copula is commonly deployed, and every reported score is an SDMetrics metric: KSComplement, CorrelationSimilarity, LogisticDetection and QualityScore. SDV supplies both the generators under test and the measuring instruments.
evidence: the abstract states that synthesis quality was benchmarked via marginal distribution fidelity (KSComplement), correlation preservation (CorrelationSimilarity), privacy (LogisticDetection) and a composite QualityScore, all of them SDMetrics metric names; the introduction states that the authors selected this pair instead of GAN-based alternatives like CTGAN (reference 1) or CopulaGAN because of the sample-size constraints typical of environmental field monitoring, both the Gaussian copula and TVAE being documented as stable under N < 500; the section on operating principles states that the Gaussian copula is frequently deployed through packages such as the Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) and characterizes a joint multivariate distribution by isolating marginals from the latent dependency structure; the reported results give CorrelationSimilarity 0.9633 for the copula against 0.9482 for TVAE and KSComplement 0.8596 against 0.8742

title: HT-Fed-GAN: Federated Generative Model for Decentralized Tabular Data Synthesis
summary: Carries tabular synthesis into federated learning, where no party sees the whole table and the two preprocessing steps CTGAN relies on both assume global statistics. The paper proposes Fed-VB-GMM, a federated variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture that learns the multimodal structure of a continuous column across clients so mode-specific normalization can be applied without centralizing data, plus a federated encoding of categorical columns, and trains the resulting HT-Fed-GAN with a Wasserstein objective and gradient penalty. Its privacy analysis mounts a customized membership inference attack in which the CTGAN package itself is the attack model. HT-Fed-GAN is a named variant built directly on CTGAN: the paper states that the architecture of its GAN follows CTGAN's, adopts CTGAN's conditional vector to encode the selected category during conditional sampling, and reworks CTGAN's mode-specific normalization as the federated component it contributes.
evidence: the related-work section describes CTGAN (reference 12) as state-of-the-art work for synthesizing tabular data proposing mode-specific normalization, a conditional generator and training-by-sampling; the method section states that in a centralized setting the state-of-the-art model performs VB-GMM to learn a Gaussian mixture in a continuous column and then applies mode-specific normalization, that federated learning has no global overview of data statistics, and that the authors therefore propose Fed-VB-GMM; the same section states that a conditional vector from reference 12 is used to encode the selected category during conditional sampling; the architecture paragraph states that the architecture of the GAN model follows the architecture of CTGAN and is trained with the WGAN objective with gradient penalty; the privacy analysis states that the authors choose ctgan (reference 12) as the attack model for the customized membership inference attack

title: An Understanding of the Vulnerability of Datasets to Disparate Membership Inference Attacks
summary: Studies why membership inference attacks succeed unevenly across the class-based subsets of a dataset rather than uniformly, and tests whether the disparity can be engineered away by hardening the data itself, through feature reduction based on correlation thresholds or on manifold structure and through class balancing by oversampling or undersampling. CTGAN is the oversampler: it was chosen over ADASYN and SMOTE because those rely on linear connections between observations while CTGAN learns the distribution of the subset being sampled, and the combination of manifold-based feature reduction with CTGAN oversampling is the best-performing treatment, cutting disparate attack accuracy while leaving victim model performance effectively unchanged. SDV's generator is thus run as one experimental treatment inside a study about attack vulnerability rather than as the paper's subject.
evidence: the methods section states that the third class-balancing method was an oversampling method using a conditional tabular generative adversarial network (CTGAN), reference 69, chosen to provide an equal number of observations in classes while maintaining the same data structure, and that other methods such as ADASYN and SMOTE rely more on linear connections between observations while CTGAN learns the original distribution of the subset of data to be sampled; the conclusions state that the best results came from a manifold theory-based feature reduction combined with CTGAN oversampling, reducing disparate attack accuracy by 0.02 on average with 19 percent of class subsets made more secure and 1 percent more vulnerable; reference 69 is Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni, Modeling tabular data using conditional GAN, NeurIPS 2019; no implementation library is named for CTGAN, while scikit-learn and TensorFlow are named for the other components

title: A Multi-Agent Intrusion Detection System Optimized by a Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach with a Dataset Enlarged Using a Generative Model to Reduce the Bias Effect
venue: Journal of Sensor and Actuator Networks
summary: Attacks the bias that a heavily imbalanced insider-threat dataset introduces into intrusion detection, by pairing synthetic attack generation with a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning setup in which an attacker and a defender agent train against each other on the CMU-CERT data. CTGAN generates the additional attack records, with its hyperparameters tuned by a tree-structured Parzen estimator, and the paper's two empirical claims both rest on it: that the probability mass functions of the synthetic insider threats closely match those of the real data, and that balancing the dataset with CTGAN output significantly improves detection performance. The authors present the combination of CTGAN generation with multi-agent intrusion detection as the gap in the literature they fill, so SDV's generator is one of the two halves of the contribution.
evidence: the abstract states that the authors considered the Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN), with its hyperparameters optimized using the tree-structured Parzen estimator, to balance the CMU-CERT insider threat dataset of discrete-value and continuous-value columns, and showed that the mean absolute errors between the probability mass functions of the actual and generated data are small; the introduction states that the approach is inspired by Xu et al. reference [6] and first generates novel realistic synthetic data using the CTGAN, and that no prior work was found combining generation of attack data using the CTGAN with intrusion detection in a multi-agent environment with insider threats; the results state that when the dataset is balanced by incorporating the attacks generated by the CTGAN, the performance of the intrusion detection system can be significantly increased

title: A Comparative Study to Predict Bearing Degradation Using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), Tabular Generative Adversarial Networks (TGAN) and Machine Learning Models
summary: Predicts bearing degradation from vibration signals under the constraint that run-to-failure experiments are expensive, so the training set is small. Vibration is decomposed by discrete wavelet transform with the base wavelet chosen by mutual information, a generative model is fitted to the resulting wavelet coefficients and sampled for artificial coefficients, statistical features are computed from real and artificial coefficients alike, and ensemble bagged trees and Gaussian process regression are trained on the combined feature vector, reaching an average RMSE of 0.0045. The generator is TGAN, credited in the text to Lei Xu and Kalyan Veeramachaneni and cited as arXiv 1811.11264, so the SDV-family model actually run here is CTGAN's predecessor rather than CTGAN, and it is the production generator of the pipeline.
evidence: the abstract states that tabular generative adversarial networks (TGAN) are used to generate the artificial coefficients after discrete wavelet transform, that statistical features are calculated from the real DWT coefficients and from the artificial data generated by TGAN, and that the constructed feature vector trains ensemble bagged tree and Gaussian process regression models; the methods section states that in this study tabular generative adversarial networks (TGAN), developed by Lei Xu and Kalyan Veeramachaneni, reference [37], used a single table of numerical and categorical variables to find the data distribution and generate fake data; reference 37 is Xu, L. and Veeramachaneni, K., Synthesizing tabular data using generative adversarial networks, arXiv:1811.11264, 2018; CTGAN is never named anywhere in the paper

title: Wearable Data Generation Using Time-Series Generative Adversarial Networks for Hydration Monitoring
summary: Generates synthetic wearable biosignals for hydration monitoring, where collecting labelled data means running controlled dehydration studies on human subjects, and evaluates whether a time-series GAN can stand in for that collection. The authors adopt TimeGAN, which is specific to sequential data, rather than a tabular generator, and assess the output on distributional similarity and downstream classification. CTGAN enters only as prior art: Xu et al. is cited for the general problem that tabular data mixes discrete and continuous columns, that such mixtures require applying both softmax and tanh at the generator output, and that modelling them realistically is non-trivial. Nothing from SDV is run, so the entry records CTGAN as the tabular line of work the paper departs from in choosing a time-series architecture.
evidence: the related-work section groups Xu et al., 2019 with other machine-learning approaches that learn the distribution of real data and then sample it; the following paragraph states that GANs have been used to generate other types of data such as tabular data with discrete and continuous values (Xu et al., 2019) and that this study instead investigates a variant of GAN specific for time-series data (Yoon et al., 2019); the method section states that to generate a mix of discrete and continuous data simultaneously GANs must apply both softmax and tanh on the output (Xu et al., 2019) and that modeling this kind of mixed tabular data is a non-trivial task; the paper contains three references to Xu et al. and no SDV-family model is trained

title: SynthCheck: A Dashboard for Synthetic Data Quality Assessment
summary: Observes that synthetic data quality tooling is mostly Python packages producing static reports, and builds SynthCheck, a graphical dashboard that walks a clinical user through resemblance, utility and privacy checks interactively, demonstrated on a cohort where missing values are first imputed by multiple imputation. Its survey of comparable tools opens with the Synthetic Data Vault, credited to Patki et al. and described through its SDGym and metrics modules as a package that both generates and evaluates synthetic data with a report but no interface, which is the gap SynthCheck fills. SDV is also one of the two generators run to produce the data the dashboard is demonstrated on, alongside HealthGAN, and is compared against it on correlation structure, outlier behaviour under local outlier factor, PCA variance and UMAP projections. SDV is therefore both a benchmark for the tool and the production generator of half its case study.
evidence: table 1, listing tools that evaluate synthetic data utility, resemblance and privacy, has the Synthetic Data Vault (Patki et al., 2016) as its first row, glossed as its SDGym and SDGMetrics module, a Python package to generate and evaluate synthetic data covering resemblance and privacy, with no GUI but a report; the case study states that to generate synthetic data the authors select two approaches, Health GAN (Yale et al., 2020) and Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) (Patki et al., 2016), and that the SDV method learns statistical information from the original dataset to create the generative model; table 2 reports HealthGAN against SDV on Pearson correlation, normalized contingency table, LOF and PCA; the discussion states that both methods fail to replicate outlier behaviour and that SDV's synthetic data does not cover some small portions of the original dataset in the UMAP projection. The paper writes the metrics module as SDGMetrics

title: FEST: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Synthetic Tabular Data
summary: Argues that synthetic tabular data is usually judged on a handful of privacy measures such as distance to closest record and nearest neighbour distance ratio, which say little on their own, and assembles FEST, a framework pulling distance-based, attack-based and utility metrics into one evaluation run so the privacy and utility of a generator can be read together. Six generators are implemented and run across the datasets to exercise the framework: CTGAN, Gaussian Copula, CopulaGAN, TVAE, a Gaussian mixture, and a random sampler included as a deliberately leaky control. Four of the six are SDV synthesizers, and the reported tables compare them metric by metric, with distance to closest record highest for CTGAN and nearest neighbour distance ratio highest for CopulaGAN. The SDV family therefore constitutes the bulk of the empirical program the framework is validated on.
evidence: the methods section states that to validate the framework across different data generation techniques the study implements and evaluates Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), Gaussian Mixture, Gaussian Copula, CopulaGAN, TVAE and a Random Model, generating for each a synthetic dataset the same size as the original; the introduction notes that existing studies rely mainly on limited privacy metrics such as Distance of Closest Record and Nearest Neighbor Distance Ratio, citing Xu et al., 2019 among others; the results state that NNDR was highest for CopulaGAN while DCR was highest for CTGAN, and that the Random model posed the highest attack-based risk; table 3 reports Wasserstein, KS, pairwise and Spearman correlation, mutual information and Jensen-Shannon values for CopulaGAN, CTGAN, Gaussian Copula, the Gaussian mixture, TVAE and the random model
